objectives: Apply the social-determinants framework + ACEs evidence to child health.
Recognize + respond to child abuse + neglect with safeguarding systems.
Understand global child health programs + the post-2000 mortality decline.

slides.title: Social determinants + ACEs: the science of upstream child health
slides.body:
**Social determinants of health (SDOH)** — conditions in which children are born, grow, live, learn, + play that shape health outcomes more powerfully than clinical care alone. WHO Commission on Social Determinants (Marmot Review 2008, 2010 *Fair Society Healthy Lives*): 'health follows a social gradient' — at every step down the socioeconomic ladder, health worsens.

**Marmot social gradient applied to pediatrics**: poverty + neighborhood disadvantage predict infant mortality, low birth weight, asthma, obesity, dental decay, injury, school readiness, + adult chronic disease. Effects are graded — not just at the bottom — + cumulate across the life-course.

**Key determinants in child health**:
- **Poverty** — ~16% of US children (2022); strongest single SDOH predictor. Material deprivation, parental stress, food + housing insecurity, neighborhood violence, lower-quality education + healthcare.
- **Housing** — instability, eviction, lead, mold, overcrowding. *Matthew Desmond's* *Evicted* documented eviction's downstream effects. Section 8, Housing First, + medical-legal partnerships intervene.
- **Food insecurity** — ~13% of US households with children. **Hunger Vital Signs** 2-question screen ('Within the past 12 months we worried whether our food would run out before we got money to buy more' / '... the food we bought just didn't last'). SNAP + WIC + school meal programs. Food insecurity linked to anemia, obesity (paradoxical), developmental delay, mental-health symptoms.
- **Education** — early childhood education (Head Start, Perry Preschool) yields decades-long benefits (Heckman ROI ~7-13× per dollar). High-quality early ed reduces special education, crime, teen pregnancy + improves earnings.
- **Neighborhood + structural racism** — segregation, redlining, environmental injustice (lead, air pollution, heat exposure). Black/Hispanic/Indigenous US children face systematically worse pediatric outcomes; AAP 2019 statement names racism as a child-health threat.

**Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) — Felitti, Anda et al. (CDC + Kaiser, 1998)**: 17,000+ adults answered 10 questions about childhood abuse (physical, sexual, emotional), neglect (physical, emotional), + household dysfunction (substance use, mental illness, incarceration, parental separation, IPV). ACE score (0-10) showed a **graded relationship** to adult disease: heart disease, stroke, cancer, COPD, diabetes, depression, suicide, substance use, early death. ACE ≥ 4 → ~12× suicide risk, 4-7× alcohol/drug risk, 2× cancer + heart disease.

**Mechanism: toxic stress (Shonkoff + Center on the Developing Child at Harvard)**: distinction between positive stress, tolerable stress, + toxic stress (prolonged adversity without buffering relationships). Toxic stress in childhood disrupts HPA + amygdala + prefrontal-cortex development → lifelong dysregulation of inflammation, metabolism, executive function. Jack Shonkoff's framework + Harvard CDC briefs popularized the science + drove policy.

**Buffering — safe stable nurturing relationships (SSNRs)**: a single supportive adult relationship can buffer toxic stress (Werner Kauai longitudinal cohort + Masten ordinary magic). This is the mechanism behind home visiting (Olds NFP — Nurse-Family Partnership), early childhood education, mental-health treatment of caregivers, + relational pediatrics.

**Pediatric SDOH screening + response**: AAP + Bright Futures recommend screening for food insecurity, housing, financial strain, IPV, parental depression, ACEs + family history. Tools: WE CARE survey, IHELP, Hunger Vital Signs, EPDS for maternal depression, ACE-IQ. Response: refer to community resources, medical-legal partnerships, social work, home visiting, parenting programs, mental-health care for caregivers + child.

slides.title: Child protection: abuse, neglect, + safeguarding systems
slides.body:
**C. Henry Kempe + the battered child syndrome (1962)**: Kempe + colleagues' *JAMA* paper 'The Battered-Child Syndrome' named child physical abuse as a medical diagnosis + galvanized US state mandatory-reporting laws (all 50 states by 1967). Child Abuse Prevention + Treatment Act (CAPTA, 1974) established federal framework. **Child abuse pediatrics** became an ABP subspecialty in **2009** — direct lineage from Kempe.

**Forms of child maltreatment**:
- **Physical abuse**: bruises in non-mobile infants (TEN-4-FACESp rule), fractures (rib, metaphyseal, multiple ages — Caffey + Kempe's foundational radiology), burns, abusive head trauma (shaken baby + impact).
- **Sexual abuse**: ~1 in 5 girls, 1 in 7-13 boys by 18 (varies by study). Most perpetrators known to victim. Often disclosed gradually; physical exam typically normal. Child Advocacy Centers (CACs) provide forensic interview + medical exam + mental-health care.
- **Neglect**: most common form (~75% of CPS cases). Failure to provide adequate food, shelter, supervision, medical care, education. Often intertwined with poverty — distinguish neglect from material deprivation.
- **Emotional abuse**: harder to identify; verbal degradation, intimidation, rejection, terrorizing.
- **Medical child abuse (Munchausen syndrome by proxy / FII)**: caregiver fabricates or induces illness in child — falsification, induction (drugs, infection), false symptom reports. Roy Meadow's 1977 *Lancet* description (later controversial in court cases); now framed as 'medical child abuse' or 'factitious disorder imposed on another'. Pediatricians must vigilantly differentiate from genuine complex disease + caregiver anxiety.
- **Online + commercial sexual exploitation**: trafficking, online enticement, child sexual abuse material — emerging vectors.

**Red flags for non-accidental injury**:
- Bruises in non-mobile infants ('those who don't cruise rarely bruise').
- Injuries inconsistent with developmental ability or history.
- Multiple injuries of varying ages.
- Delayed care-seeking.
- Changing or implausible histories.
- Specific patterns: rib + metaphyseal corner fractures, posterior rib fractures, retinal hemorrhages with subdural in abusive head trauma.

**Evaluation**:
- Skeletal survey (under ~2-3 yr) — 20+ films per AAP protocol.
- Neuroimaging (CT head urgent; MRI for detail).
- Ophthalmology (retinal hemorrhages).
- Hepatic + pancreatic enzymes (occult abdominal trauma).
- Coagulation studies (rule out bleeding disorder).
- Sexual-abuse exam by trained provider (SANE/CAPS).

**Mandatory reporting + safeguarding**: all US states (+ most countries) require physicians, teachers, social workers + others to report suspected maltreatment to **CPS / DCF / Department of Children + Family Services**. The threshold is reasonable suspicion, not certainty. Reporters are immune from liability when reporting in good faith. **Failing to report carries legal + professional consequences.**

**UK + International**: UK system uses **safeguarding** language; Lord Laming reviews after the Victoria Climbié (2003) + Baby P (2008) cases reformed multi-agency working. Patricia Wood's work + the Wood Report (UK, 2016) reshaped local safeguarding child boards into multi-agency safeguarding arrangements (MASAs). UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) is foundational global framework — ratified by every country except the US.

**Trauma-informed care**: clinical practice that recognizes high prevalence of trauma + adjusts approach — safety, transparency, choice, collaboration, empowerment. AAP + SAMHSA guidelines. Reduces re-traumatization + improves engagement.

**Prevention**: home visiting (Olds NFP — Nurse-Family Partnership reduces maltreatment ~50% + adolescent crime/substance use in RCTs), parenting programs (Triple P, Incredible Years), economic supports (Earned Income Tax Credit reduces maltreatment), reducing parental substance use, school-based prevention curricula.

slides.title: Global child health: IMNCI, vaccines, + the mortality decline
slides.body:
**Global under-5 mortality** fell from **93/1000 in 1990 to 38/1000 in 2021** — a ~60% reduction, with ~5 million children under 5 dying in 2021 vs ~12.5 million in 1990. Largest sustained child-mortality improvement in history. **Sustainable Development Goal 3.2** targets < 25/1000 by 2030.

**Drivers of the decline (1990-2020)**:
- **Vaccines** — measles deaths fell > 95%; Hib + pneumococcal + rotavirus rollouts; polio near-eradication.
- **ORS + zinc** for diarrhea (since 1971 Mahalanabis + Cash).
- **Insecticide-treated bednets + ACTs** for malaria.
- **Antiretroviral therapy** for HIV — pediatric HIV mortality + mother-to-child transmission drastically reduced.
- **Skilled birth attendance** + **emergency obstetric care** reduced neonatal + maternal mortality.
- **Breastfeeding + nutrition** programs (IYCF, RUTF for severe acute malnutrition).
- **Improved water + sanitation** + community case management.
- **GAVI (Vaccine Alliance, founded 2000)** — public-private partnership accelerating low-income-country vaccine access; ~1 billion children vaccinated, ~17 million deaths averted by 2022.
- **Global Fund** + Bill + Melinda Gates Foundation funding shifts.

**Persistent challenges (post-2015)**:
- Sub-Saharan Africa + South Asia still have highest mortality; progress slowing in some regions.
- Neonatal deaths now ~47% of under-5 mortality (down from ~37%) — proportionally larger as post-neonatal mortality fell faster.
- Pneumonia + diarrhea + malaria still leading killers in children outside the neonatal period.
- Conflict + climate + economic shocks disrupt programs (COVID-19 caused largest immunization disruption in 30 yr).
- Stunting affects ~149M children globally (UNICEF 2022); wasting ~45M.

**IMCI / IMNCI (Integrated Management of Childhood Illness, WHO/UNICEF 1995 + Integrated Management of Newborn + Childhood Illness 2003)**: protocol-based primary-care approach for resource-limited settings. Algorithms address common causes of child mortality (pneumonia, diarrhea, malaria, measles, malnutrition) + integrate vaccinations + counseling. Implemented in ~100+ countries; meta-analyses show modest mortality reduction + significant quality-of-care improvement.

**Black + Bhutta + Lancet Child Survival Series (2003 + updates)**: landmark *Lancet* series led by **Robert Black** (Johns Hopkins) modeled how scaling proven interventions could prevent 60% of child deaths. Reframed global child health priorities + drove investment. The 2003 series + subsequent Lancet Maternal + Child Nutrition + Stillbirth + Every Newborn series shape global agenda.

**UNICEF *State of the World's Children* report (annual since 1980)**: thematic flagship publication. Topics include nutrition, immunization, gender, mental health (2021), climate (2022). Tracks progress + accountability. UNICEF (founded 1946, co-founded by Robert Debré) remains the world's leading agency for children's rights + welfare.

**Climate + future**: WHO + UNICEF estimate the climate crisis will undo decades of child-health gains without rapid mitigation + adaptation. Heat, vector-borne disease shifts (malaria, dengue), food + water insecurity, displacement, + mental-health effects fall hardest on children. Lancet Countdown on Health + Climate Change tracks indicators annually. Pinto + others have linked climate, displacement, + pediatric health outcomes in policy frameworks for post-2030 strategies.

question.question: Trace how a high ACE score (≥ 4) leads to elevated adult heart-disease risk through toxic stress.
question.goal: Connect childhood adversity → biology → adult disease.

steps.prompt: What does the Felitti + Anda 1998 study show?

acceptedAnswers: graded dose-response between ACE score + adult disease (heart disease, cancer, depression, addiction, early death)

steps.reveal: Felitti, Anda et al. (1998, *AJPM*) surveyed 17,000+ Kaiser members on 10 ACE categories. They documented a **graded, dose-response relationship** between ACE score + adult diseases. ACE ≥ 4 vs 0 was associated with ~2× heart disease + cancer, ~4× depression, ~7× alcoholism, ~12× suicide. The effect persisted after adjusting for confounders.

steps.prompt: What is the biological mechanism (Shonkoff toxic stress)?

acceptedAnswers: prolonged HPA axis activation + altered amygdala/PFC development + chronic inflammation + dysregulated metabolism

steps.reveal: Jack Shonkoff (Center on the Developing Child, Harvard) distinguishes **positive** stress (brief, buffered), **tolerable** stress (significant but with relational support), + **toxic** stress (prolonged, unbuffered). Toxic stress in early life dysregulates HPA axis (cortisol), alters amygdala + prefrontal-cortex development (impaired emotion regulation, executive function), drives chronic low-grade inflammation, + reshapes metabolic + immune setpoints — the biological pathway from ACE to disease.

steps.prompt: How does adult heart disease arise from these mechanisms?

acceptedAnswers: behavioral mediators (smoking, obesity, substance use) + biological (inflammation, BP, insulin resistance) → atherosclerosis + CVD

steps.reveal: Two pathways: (1) **behavioral mediators** — toxic-stress + emotional dysregulation → smoking, substance use, overeating, sedentary behavior, sleep dysregulation, all CVD risk factors. (2) **Biological mediators** — chronic inflammation (elevated CRP, IL-6), elevated BP, insulin resistance, endothelial dysfunction, accelerated cellular aging (shorter telomeres). Both pathways converge on atherosclerosis, hypertension, myocardial events. Mediation analyses show partial but not complete explanation by behavior alone.

steps.prompt: What buffers the effect + what is the policy implication?

acceptedAnswers: safe stable nurturing relationships (SSNRs); home visiting (Olds NFP), early childhood education, parenting support, treating caregiver mental illness

steps.reveal: Buffering by **safe stable nurturing relationships (SSNRs)** — even a single supportive adult — moderates ACE effects (Werner Kauai cohort; Masten 'ordinary magic'; CDC SSNR framework). Policy: invest in **home visiting** (Olds NFP — Nurse-Family Partnership reduced child maltreatment ~50% + adolescent crime in RCTs); early childhood education; treating caregiver mental illness + substance use; parenting programs; economic supports (EITC reduces maltreatment). Pediatrics moves upstream — primary prevention of toxic stress is among the highest-leverage interventions in medicine.

question.question: What is the legacy of Henry Kempe's 1962 *JAMA* paper on the battered child syndrome?
options: Kempe, Silverman, Steele, Droegemueller, + Silver (*JAMA* 1962) — **'The Battered-Child Syndrome'** — named child physical abuse as a medical diagnosis with characteristic radiographic + clinical findings. The paper galvanized US **state mandatory-reporting laws** (all 50 states by 1967) + federal **CAPTA (Child Abuse Prevention + Treatment Act, 1974)**. Kempe founded the International Society for Prevention of Child Abuse + Neglect (ISPCAN). **Child abuse pediatrics** became an ABP subspecialty in 2009. The paper established that child protection is a core pediatric responsibility, transforming both clinical practice + child-welfare law.
First description of failure to thrive.

Within 5 years all 50 US states had mandatory-reporting laws; CAPTA followed in 1974; child abuse pediatrics became an ABP subspecialty in 2009. Kempe transformed both pediatrics + child welfare law + established safeguarding as a core pediatric duty.

question.question: A 4-month-old presents to the ED with a spiral femur fracture + a parent's vague history. The infant is non-mobile. How do you proceed?
question.scenario: Apply the non-accidental injury workup + reporting framework.
question.modelAnswer: High suspicion for non-accidental injury (NAI): spiral femur fracture in a non-mobile infant is uncommon for accidental injury + 'those who don't cruise rarely bruise/break'. Maintain calm + non-judgmental clinical demeanor. Workup per AAP: (1) detailed history — onset, witnesses, prior care; document carefully + verbatim. (2) Thorough physical exam — full skin survey, mucous membranes, frenulum, palpation for occult fractures, growth parameters. (3) **Skeletal survey** (20+ films per AAP, repeat at 2 weeks to identify healing fractures missed on first pass). (4) Neuroimaging — head CT urgently or MRI for occult abusive head trauma in children < 2 yr. (5) Ophthalmology for retinal hemorrhages. (6) Hepatic + pancreatic enzymes (occult abdominal trauma). (7) Coagulation studies + bleeding-disorder labs to rule out medical mimics. (8) Consider osteogenesis imperfecta + metabolic bone disease workup. (9) Consult **child abuse pediatrics** specialist if available. (10) **Report to CPS / DCF** based on reasonable suspicion — not certainty; mandatory reporter immunity applies. (11) Consider hospital admission for safety + workup completion. (12) Engage social work + trauma-informed approach with family. Document objectively without speculative narrative. The threshold is reasonable suspicion of abuse; CPS + law enforcement complete the determination.
question.rubric: Recognizes NAI red flags, orders skeletal survey + appropriate imaging + labs, reports to CPS, consults child abuse pediatrics, + uses trauma-informed approach.

question.question: Under-5 mortality fell from 93/1000 in 1990 to 38/1000 in 2021. Approximately how many child lives are saved annually if 2021 mortality applied to the 1990 birth cohort (~135 million births)?
question.explanation: Rate difference = (93 − 38) / 1000 = 0.055. Applied to 135 million births: 0.055 × 135,000,000 ≈ 7.4 million lives saved annually compared with 1990 mortality at the same birth volume. UNICEF + IGME estimates align: ~12.5M under-5 deaths in 1990 vs ~5M in 2021 — roughly 7.5M fewer per year. Drivers include vaccines, ORS, skilled birth, antibiotics, bednets, antiretrovirals, + nutrition programs. SDG 3.2 targets < 25/1000 by 2030.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why pediatricians screen for social determinants + ACEs even when 'medical' presentation is the chief complaint.
question.rubric: Mentions: (1) Marmot's social gradient + Felitti/Anda's ACE study showed that childhood adversity + poverty drive disease across the life course more powerfully than most clinical interventions. (2) Shonkoff's toxic-stress framework explains the biological mechanism (HPA dysregulation, brain development, chronic inflammation). (3) Single supportive relationships buffer toxic stress — pediatricians can be that adult + can connect families to community supports. (4) Screening tools (Hunger Vital Signs, WE CARE, ACE-IQ) are quick + actionable when paired with referral resources (medical-legal partnerships, food pantries, home visiting, mental-health care). (5) Treating asthma without addressing mold + tobacco exposure is ineffective; treating depression without housing stability is unsustainable. Concludes: social pediatrics is not optional — it is upstream medicine.
